Not the author, but for near-duplicates I use MinHash on character n-grams. A hash of the normalised text catches exact copies after stripping, MinHash catches the edited ones.

Normalised hash first: lowercase, strip punctuation and tone marks, collapse spaces. That removed most of them. For the rest I used MinHash with a 0.8 threshold on 5-grams of characters and checked a handful by hand.
Splitting by source is the bigger fix, I think. Even with perfect dedup, two articles from the same outlet share style and recycled phrases, and a model can learn the outlet instead of the topic.
MinHash is worth knowing. We use it to dedup sensor event logs too. The datasketch package makes it a few lines in Python.

title: Versioning a Vue design system without drowning consumers in releases
body: Our Vue design system is published as an npm package. Every component change triggers a version bump, and consumers complain about too many releases, 2 to 3 a week. Options: batch weekly, use a canary channel for the fast ones, or split into separate packages by component group. What do other small teams do for versioning a design system without drowning the people who consume it?

comments.body: Strict semver, and let the changelog say what changed. Consumers who do not want frequent updates can pin. Frequent releases are not a problem if each one is safe. Generate the changelog from commit messages so it is not a chore.

Security angle: frequent releases are fine, but consumers should use a lockfile and review the diff of the dist. Weekly batching makes each diff bigger and harder to review, the opposite of what you would think.

Weekly batching with a changelog worked for us. Fixes go out immediately as patches, features batch on Thursday. Consumers know when to expect them, and that predictability matters more than the number.
As a consumer of a similar system in React, what annoys me is not the count but breaking changes in minor versions. If your releases never break me, release as often as you like.
Use Changesets or similar tooling to collect changes and release when someone decides. The tool does the bookkeeping, humans decide the cadence. Do not tie releases to every merge.
Agree with Henriette. A visual change in a component is a breaking change for anyone with screenshot checks, even if the props are unchanged. Do you treat a spacing change as minor?
Separate packages per component group is more overhead than it looks: imports across them, peer versions drifting. I would avoid it unless more than one team consumes different parts.
Canary channel: publish every merge under a next tag and let willing consumers use it, then cut stable weekly. We did this with a shared Rust crate across firmware and the complaints dropped to zero.
A deprecation policy also helps: tell consumers a component stays for two minors after it is replaced, not forever.

Not a design systems person, but our ML library had the same complaint and what worked was a public roadmap note: next release date and what is in it. People complain less when they can see it coming.

title: Wallet transfer screen and backgrounding mid-request in React Native
body: Mobile wallet in React Native. The balance lives in a Zustand store and I refetch it after every transaction. The transfer button disables during the request, but if the user backgrounds the app mid-request, on return the screen shows the old balance and the button is enabled again. I handle it with an AppState listener that refetches when the app becomes active. Is that enough? I worry about a second submission if the first request actually succeeded.

comments.body: Refetch on active is fine for display. For the second tap, add a server rule: if the same recipient and amount arrive within 30 seconds, ask for confirmation instead of silently processing. Also persist the pending transfer to storage. The OS can kill the app while it is backgrounded, and the new launch has no idea a request was in flight.

title: Formulaire d'inscription en plusieurs étapes : l'état reste après la soumission
body: Composable Vue pour un formulaire d'inscription à l'université en plusieurs étapes (4 étapes, 30 champs). L'état est dans un reactive() global dans un fichier à part, donc partagé entre tous les composants, mais il persiste après la soumission : un deuxième étudiant sur le même poste de la scolarité voit les données du premier. Je remets à zéro à la fin, mais pas si la personne ferme l'onglet. Je ne sais pas si je dois passer à Pinia ou à provide/inject.

comments.body: Côté serveur aussi, attention : si le formulaire enregistre un brouillon par poste ou par session, un autre étudiant peut le reprendre. Les brouillons doivent être liés à la personne connectée, pas au navigateur.

Un reactive() global dans un module, c'est un singleton : il vit tant que la page vit. Pinia ne change rien à ça. Ce qu'il te faut, c'est un reset à l'entrée du formulaire et pas seulement à la sortie, comme ça fermer l'onglet ne laisse rien. Et pas de localStorage pour des données personnelles sur un poste partagé.

title: LoRA on a 1.3B model for extracting sales-dip reasons, loss drops but output is worse
body: Fine-tuning a 1.3B model with LoRA on about 8,000 Arabic and French notes written by store managers, to extract the reason for a sales dip. Validation loss keeps dropping, but the extraction is worse than a regex plus a small classifier I already have. Is LoRA the wrong tool here, or is my rank (r=8) too low?

comments.body: Loss on what? If it is next-token loss over the full notes, it will keep dropping while extraction quality stalls. Measure the actual task, exact match on the extracted reason, every few hundred steps.
Seconding that. And read 20 outputs by hand. When I did, I found the model had learned to copy the first sentence of the note.

Treat the regex plus classifier as a baseline you must beat, as you already do. If 8,000 notes give you 90 percent with that, the language model is only worth it for the long tail of notes the regex misses. Route the easy ones to the cheap path.

title: Keying a reconciliation map when reversals reuse the original reference
body:
Go job that reconciles M-Pesa statement lines against our ledger entries. Both sides go into maps keyed by transaction reference, then I walk the statement and mark what agrees. About 60,000 lines a day, runs in 2 seconds. What I doubt is the key: reversals reuse the original reference with a negative amount, so the later line overwrites the earlier one in the map. I was thinking of something like this:

key := ref + "|" + kind + "|" + strconv.Itoa(seq)

but seq is not in the statement. What would you key on?

title: fielddrain 1.2: adaptive batching for MQTT field readings
body: fielddrain 1.2 is out. It is a Go service that collects readings from field devices over MQTT and writes them to Postgres in batches. Changes: batch size now adapts to insert latency, readings with a device timestamp more than 24 hours off are quarantined instead of dropped, and a --dry-run flag prints what would be written. Still rough: client certificate rotation needs a restart, the Prometheus metric names will change in 1.3, and Postgres is the only target.

comments.body: Where does the quarantine table live? Same database? If a device clock is wrong for a month it will fill up. Is there a retention setting?
Same database, its own table, with a retention flag that defaults to 30 days. Added it in 1.2 and forgot to put it in this note.
Side question from a frontend person: is there an endpoint to see what is in quarantine, or is it SQL only? A small page for operators would be nice.
How do you stop the adaptive batch size from oscillating? We built something similar and it swung between 50 and 5,000 until we added a smoothing factor.
30 days is generous. Make sure the quarantine table has an index on received_at, or the retention delete will lock for ages on a busy table.
Any plan for SQLite as a target? We have gateways on site that buffer locally when the uplink drops.
